## 4. Academic Research & Publications

### "Security Against Fork Bomb Attack in Linux Based Systems"
- **Authors:** Krunalkumar D. Shah & Krunal V. Patel
- **Journal:** *International Journal of Research in Advent Technology (IJRAT)*, Vol. 7, No. 4, April 2019 (E-ISSN: 2321-9637).
- **DOI:** [10.32622/ijrat.74201911](https://doi.org/10.32622/ijrat.74201911)
- **Award:** Nominated for Best Paper Award in Linux research at IAENG.
- **Core Mechanism:** Proposes a hybrid mitigation model combining process exception lists, dynamic rate-checking, and process resource quarantining. When a recorded process name repeats, it runs inside a resource-quarantined sandbox for inspection rather than being permanently killed, preventing false positives on fork-heavy legitimate applications (e.g., CAD tools).
- **Benchmarks:** Tested on Xubuntu 18.04 (Kernel 4.15) with Bash fork bombs, detecting and mitigating attacks in ~44 ms at a 500-fork threshold while preserving OS availability.

## 5. Featured Projects & Open-Source Repositories

- **ChurnGPT 2.0 (`011-ChurnGPT-2.0`):** Multi-stage AI pipeline digesting CRM records, tickets, and meeting transcripts to summarise churn tickets, validate the churn reason given, and show the evidence behind each decision. Reported outcome: churn-ticket review fell from 15 minutes to 2 (an 87% efficiency gain) and 200+ tickets were processed in under 20 minutes; built in five days. Figures reported publicly by Zeni's RevOps lead, Brandon Dith-Berry.

## 7. Internship, Mentorship & Credential Verification

### Educational Programs
- **Free Internship (Selective):** 2–3 seats per cohort, ~3 months long, zero fees. Interns ship real production work and receive verified project completion certificates.
- **Paid Mentorship (Open):** ₹4,999/month (India) or $120/month (International via Wise), cancel anytime. Features weekly 1:1 sessions, custom roadmaps, code reviews, and scholarships up to 50%.
- **Separation Rule:** Mentorship participation never converts into an internship title; each certificate honestly reflects the exact program completed. Corporate training is a separate paid B2B service, distinct from both the free internship and the paid 1:1 mentorship.

### Certificate Verification System
- Public verification is accessible at `https://krunalkumar.dpdns.org/verify`.
- Every completion certificate features a unique ID (e.g., `KS-INT-2026-XXXXXX` or `KS-MEN-2026-XXXXXX`) that verifies against client-side records in `assets/data/certificates.json`.

## 8. Policies & Operational Guidelines

- **Privacy (DPDP Act 2023):** No server-side form databases; form submissions route straight to WhatsApp messages. Uses Google Analytics 4 (cookies can be opted out freely without breaking site features).
- **Terms & Rules:** Work is performed strictly on authorized accounts/devices with proven ownership. No device bypassing or unauthorized surveillance.
- **Refunds:** Mentorship includes a 100% money-back guarantee within the first 7 days of the first month. Consulting milestones not yet started are fully refundable.

## Synth & DJ desk (/labs/synth)

Three instruments sharing one mixer, all in the browser.

- **A deck for your own file.** An audio file is read with an object URL and
  routed through a MediaElementSource. It is never uploaded — the site is static
  and has nowhere to upload it to.
- **A sixteen-step drum machine** with kick, snare, clap, closed and open hat,
  70-170 BPM, scheduled against the audio clock with a lookahead window rather
  than a timer, so the pattern does not drift.
- **Five one-shot pads** (keys 1-5) for playing over a track rather than
  programming one.
- **A playable synth**: sawtooth, square, triangle or sine through a resonant
  low-pass, with attack and release, polyphonic, played with the mouse, a finger
  or the QWERTY home row laid out like a piano.
- **Every sound but your file is generated.** The drums are synthesised the same
  way the ones on /party are — a pitch-dropping sine for the kick, filtered noise
  for the hats, three noise bursts nine milliseconds apart for the clap. There
  are no samples to download and nothing to licence.
- One oscilloscope shows the summed output, so the deck and the synth are
  visibly mixing rather than merely playing at the same time.

## Colophon (/colophon)

How the site is built, and the one page that maintains itself.

- **No framework, no bundler, no CSS preprocessor and zero npm dependencies.**
  Every page is a hand-written .html file, and the file in the repository is the
  file the browser is served.
- **The deploy is allowed to refuse.** One script strips CSS comments, rewrites
  sitemap dates from git, rebuilds the search index, then verifies its own
  output — critical files present and above a size floor, the ordered list of
  CSS selectors unchanged, braces balanced, page count above a floor. Any of
  those failing throws instead of writing, and the previous deployment keeps
  serving.
- **Comments are stripped at deploy, not deleted from the repository**, because
  they carry the measurements and the rejected alternatives. Git keeps every
  comment; visitors get the smaller file.
- **Every figure on the page is counted at build time** from a data-colophon
  attribute, so adding labs or posts corrects the numbers on the next push and
  the page is never edited by hand.

## A still place (/buddha)

A contemplative page, deliberately unlike the rest of the site: an illustrated
Buddha sitting cross-legged on a lotus, a verse from the Pali Canon, and a guided
breath.

- **684 verses**, one chosen at random on load and again on every tap, never the
  same twice in a row. Sources: Dhammapada (30), Samyutta Nikaya, Anguttara
  Nikaya, Majjhima Nikaya, Itivuttaka, Udana, Sutta Nipata, Theragatha,
  Therigatha, Karaniya Metta Sutta.
- **Every verse is cited.** This matters more than it looks: a large share of the
  "Buddha quotes" in circulation are modern fabrications — "holding on to anger
  is like grasping a hot coal", "what you think, you become", "peace comes from
  within" and "three things cannot be long hidden" among them. Everything shown
  here was checked against suttacentral.net or accesstoinsight.org.
- **The breathing guide** runs 4 seconds in, 6 seconds out. The longer exhale is
  the part that settles a nervous system, and the halo and the figure breathe on
  the same cycle.
- **The figure is inline SVG**, not a photograph — the site's Content Security
  Policy is `img-src 'self'`, so an off-origin image would be blocked, and vector
  stays sharp at any size. He breathes, the halo rays turn, the light in his
  hands twinkles, and every nine seconds he opens his eyes and grins for a second
  and a half.
- **Tapping him** changes the verse, with a bounce and a burst of sparkles.
- **The sound is synthesised, never a file.** There is no audio behind this page
  to download or licence: a tanpura cycling Pa-Sa-Sa-Sa, a sustained sub, an
  inharmonic singing bowl and a bansuri-like flute are all computed in the
  browser with the Web Audio API. Nothing plays until the speaker button is
  pressed, and the choice is remembered.
- **Four settings, cycled with the T key.** Bhairavi at dawn, Yaman at dusk,
  Bhupali in the evening, and a sustained Om that drops the flute entirely for a
  lower tonic and a formant-synthesised voice. Each is a real raga with a time of
  day attached to it, and each carries its own drone tuning, tanpura, scale, bowl
  set and pacing — a slower setting is one whose silences are longer, not one
  that is quieter. Changing setting slides the drone to the new tonic rather than
  cutting. Pressing `m` toggles the breath words, unchanged.
- **Fullscreen mode** hands the entire screen to the scene.
- Nothing is collected, counted or stored. There is no sign-up.

## A loud place (/party)

The counterpart to the still place, and built to the same rules: a dance bar
that runs entirely in the browser.

- **Nothing is downloaded.** The dancers, the waiters, the guests at the tables
  and the DJ are inline SVG; the light beams, the mirror ball and its rotating
  rainbow cast are CSS gradients; the music is computed with the Web Audio API.
  There is no audio file to buffer and no track to licence.
- **The room** is a floor with six dancers — two pairs drawn in profile so they
  face each other — a DJ working both platters from behind the decks, PA stacks
  flanking the booth, and two tables in the front corners with four seated guests
  and two waiters carrying trays.
- **Four tracks, cycled with the T key**, the same shortcut as the still page:
  Midnight House (124 BPM), Neon Funk (112), Sunrise Trance (138) and Garage Skip
  (130). Each has its own key, chord movement, drum pattern, bass rhythm, lead
  motif and lead waveform.
- **It is an arrangement, not a loop.** Each track runs a thirty-two bar
  structure — intro, the bass entering, the full groove, a breakdown with the
  drums pulled out, a riser and snare roll, then the drop — because a four-bar
  loop is what makes generated music sound generated.
- **The kit** is a sine kick that pitch-drops from 160 Hz to 47, a three-burst
  noise clap, closed and open hats, a shaker, a resonant sawtooth bass with a
  sine sub beneath it, three detuned sawtooths for the chord stab, a filtered
  lead and a noise riser.
- **Nothing plays until the visitor presses the button.** Browsers require a
  gesture before audio, and the choice is remembered like the still page's.
- **Photosensitivity is treated as a hard constraint.** Every light pulse is
  locked to the beat, so at 124 BPM that is 2.07 flashes a second — below the
  three-per-second ceiling in WCAG 2.3.1 — and the lights physically cannot
  outrun the music. No full-area flash swings a large luminance step, and under
  `prefers-reduced-motion` the room holds still and nothing flashes at all.
- **The controls withdraw** when nothing has happened for a few seconds, and come
  back on any pointer, touch or keyboard activity. There is a fullscreen mode.
- Nothing is collected, counted or stored.

## Peer-to-peer chat (/labs/chat)

One of only two labs that opens a network connection — the browser-leak page
below makes a STUN request for the same WebRTC reason. Every other tool runs
entirely inside the tab with no requests of any kind; this one connects two
browsers directly to each other, and says so prominently before anything else.

- **No server.** Two browsers exchange a short code by whatever channel the two
  people already share — a chat app, an email, a note —
  and after that the connection is direct. Nothing is stored, nothing passes
  through this site, and there is no account or database behind it.
- **Why the code exists at all.** A browser cannot accept an incoming
  connection. No JavaScript API binds a socket and listens; fetch, WebSocket,
  EventSource and RTCPeerConnection all dial outward. A page that could listen
  would turn every open tab into a reachable server. So neither side can find
  the other unaided, and the first message has to be carried by hand.
- **Code size.** 243 characters for the invitation, 147 for the reply. The full
  SDP is never transmitted: 14 of its 21 lines are identical on every WebRTC
  connection and are rebuilt from a template, leaving only the ICE credentials,
  the DTLS fingerprint and the addresses.
- **Group chat** uses a star: everyone connects to the host, who repeats what it
  hears. N-1 exchanges rather than N(N-1)/2.
- **File transfer** is chunked with backpressure. No size limit in Chrome or
  Edge, where each chunk is written straight to disk; 512 MB elsewhere, where it
  has to be held in memory.
- **Voice and video are one-to-one only**, because relaying video needs a media
  server and relaying text does not.
- **Live inspector** showing ICE candidates by type, gathering and connection
  state, and which path finally carried the traffic.

## Security tools

Sixteen browser-based security tools at /labs/<name>. Each runs entirely in the
visitor's tab with no network requests, no account and no history. This is not a
privacy footnote but the design constraint: the inputs these tools take — evidence
files, production JWTs, passwords, photographs with GPS in them, raw email headers —
are precisely the data that should never be uploaded to a third party, and every
popular online equivalent does exactly that.

- /labs/hash — Hash generator & verifier. MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512 and HMAC for text or files, plus checksum verification and hash identification.
- /labs/file-inspector — File type inspector & hex viewer. Identifies a file from its magic bytes rather than its extension, and flags the mismatch. Hex dump, printable strings and an entropy graph.
- /labs/jwt — JWT decoder & verifier. Decodes a JSON Web Token, explains every claim, checks expiry and verifies HMAC signatures. The token is never transmitted.
- /labs/exif — EXIF viewer & metadata remover. Reads the camera, timestamp, serial number and GPS coordinates inside a photo, then re-encodes a stripped copy.
- /labs/email-headers — Email header analyzer. Parses the Received chain, reads SPF, DKIM and DMARC results, detects Reply-To spoofing and extracts the originating IP.
- /labs/url-inspector — URL & phishing link inspector. Takes a suspicious link apart without ever requesting it: homograph characters, buried domains, nested encoding, open redirects.
- /labs/password — Password strength checker & generator. Real entropy plus offline crack times against MD5, SHA-256, bcrypt and Argon2id. Generator uses crypto.getRandomValues.
- /labs/cert-decoder — SSL/TLS certificate decoder. Decodes an X.509 PEM without OpenSSL: subject, issuer, validity, key size, SANs, extensions and fingerprints.
- /labs/certificate-forge — Certificate & digital signature builder. The decoder in reverse: generates a real RSA-2048 or ECDSA P-256 keypair with WebCrypto, then hand-encodes a self-signed X.509 certificate, a PKCS#10 CSR and a two-certificate chain of trust, with the ASN.1/DER shown byte by byte. Also signs messages and demonstrates tamper detection. The output is verified against a real X.509 parser and parses in openssl. Nothing is uploaded.
- /labs/encoding — Encoder & decoder. Base64, Base64url, Base32, Base58, hex, URL, HTML entities, binary, decimal, Morse and JSON, with automatic format detection.
- /labs/cipher — Classical cipher playground. Caesar, ROT13, Atbash, Vigenere and XOR — and automatic cryptanalysis that breaks all of them without a key.
- /labs/steganography — Image steganography. Hides a message in the least significant bits of a PNG, extracts one, and amplifies the low-bit plane to reveal concealed data.
- /labs/regex — Regex tester & ReDoS checker. Live matching with capture groups, plus an empirical catastrophic-backtracking test and a library of security-relevant patterns.
- /labs/cvss — CVSS v3.1 calculator. The official base score formula with every metric explained and its contribution shown. Parses and emits vector strings.
- /labs/subnet — Subnet & CIDR calculator. IPv4 ranges, masks in every notation, the binary breakdown, and RFC 1918 / CGNAT / reserved-range classification.
- /labs/timestamp — Forensic timestamp converter. Reads a value under Unix, Windows FILETIME, WebKit, Apple Cocoa, HFS+ and MS-DOS epochs at once to identify which system wrote it.

## Network lookup tools

Five tools at /labs/<name> that DO make network requests, unlike the rest of Labs.
They are built on assets/js/labs/net-tool-shell.js, never tool-shell.js, whose header
promises that nothing built on it opens a connection. Each names its vendor and what
that vendor learns before any request fires; nothing fires on page load or on a
keystroke; every request is echoed on screen; and a running request count is shown.
There is no proxy — the visitor's browser contacts the vendor directly.

- /labs/dns — DNS lookup. Queries Google or Cloudflare. A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, SOA and CAA over DNS-over-HTTPS, with your choice of resolver. A browser cannot speak DNS directly - this is how it gets there.
- /labs/email-security — Email security audit. Queries Google Public DNS. Can somebody send mail pretending to be this domain? SPF, DKIM, DMARC, MTA-STS and BIMI, parsed and graded, from public DNS alone.
- /labs/ct-log — Certificate transparency. Queries SSLMate Cert Spotter. Every certificate ever logged for a domain, and the subdomains printed on them - discovered without sending a single packet to the target.
- /labs/rdap — Domain registration (RDAP). Queries the authoritative registry. Registration date, expiry, transfer locks and DNSSEC. Classic WHOIS needs a raw TCP socket; RDAP speaks HTTPS, so there is no proxy in the path.
- /labs/breach-check — Password breach check. Queries Have I Been Pwned. Is this password in a known breach? Only five characters of its hash are sent, and the comparison happens in your tab. k-anonymity, not a promise.

## Digital forensics tools

Six file-forensics tools at /labs/<name>, on the same offline shell as the
security tools: you drop a file and it is parsed in your tab, never uploaded.
They read real container and dump formats rather than guessing.

- /labs/har-analyzer — HAR analyzer. Parses a browser HAR capture: every request, timing waterfall, headers, cookies, sizes and a flag for anything sent in the clear or leaking credentials.
- /labs/sqlite-browser — SQLite database browser. Opens a .sqlite/.db file with a real SQLite engine (sql.js), lists tables and schema, and runs read-only SQL against it — all in the browser.
- /labs/archive-inspector — Archive inspector. Reads the structure of ZIP, TAR and GZIP archives without extracting: entries, sizes, compression, timestamps and ZIP64, plus zip-bomb and path-traversal warnings.
- /labs/pcap-analyzer — PCAP analyzer. Decodes a packet capture (pcap/pcapng): Ethernet/IP/TCP/UDP layers, conversations, DNS and HTTP, and plaintext credentials carved from the stream.
- /labs/memory-strings — Memory string extractor. Carves printable ASCII and UTF-16 strings from a raw memory or process dump, with length filtering and pattern highlighting for URLs, keys and paths.
- /labs/registry-viewer — Windows registry viewer. Parses a raw Windows registry hive file into its key/value tree, decoding every value type, without a Windows machine.

## Interactive visualisers

Twelve visualisers at /labs/<name>. Where the tools are request/response, these
run live: a canvas, a simulation, an algorithm stepped one frame at a time. Many
share a chassis (assets/js/labs/viz/multi-shell.js) giving tabs, a transport
(reset/back/play/step/end), a speed control and a compare table. Every algorithmic
core is tested against known-answer vectors in a Node harness under _labtools/.
All run entirely client-side.

- /labs/os-algorithms — Operating system algorithm visualiser. CPU scheduling (FCFS, SJF, SRTF, round robin, priority), page replacement (FIFO, LRU, OPT, clock, LFU), disk scheduling (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK, C-LOOK), memory allocation (first/best/worst/next fit) and the Banker safety check — 26 algorithms stepped one time unit at a time with every algorithm compared on the same input. Reproduces Belady’s anomaly.
- /labs/cryptography — Cryptography visualiser. AES-128 stepped through all 40 transformations with a live avalanche measurement, SHA-256 across its 64 compression rounds, and Diffie-Hellman, RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange with small checkable numbers plus a working brute-force attacker. Teaching implementations, verified against FIPS-197 and FIPS-180-4 test vectors.
- /labs/regex-engine — Regex engine & ReDoS visualiser. A regular expression engine built from scratch: recursive descent parser, Thompson NFA construction, subset construction to a DFA, and a backtracking matcher, all steppable. The ReDoS panel measures backtracking cost against input length versus the linear state-machine engines. All three engines are differentially tested against JavaScript RegExp.
- /labs/buffer-overflow — Stack buffer overflow visualiser. A stack overflow drawn byte by byte on a real downward-growing stack: a string copy overwrites the saved frame pointer and return address, control flow is hijacked to injected shellcode (a diagram, never executed), then a stack canary catches it. A defences panel shows what NX and ASLR stop and how each is bypassed.
- /labs/tcp-congestion — TCP visualiser. The three-way handshake and four-way close with real sequence/acknowledgement arithmetic, the TCP state machine walked by both endpoints, and TCP Reno congestion control simulated round trip by round trip — slow start, congestion avoidance, fast recovery and timeout collapse, plotted as the classic sawtooth. Checked against RFC 793 examples.
- /labs/word-cloud — Word cloud generator. Paste text and the most frequent words are sized biggest and spiral-packed into shape masks (heart, star, circle, diamond, cloud), with colour palettes and font choices, downloadable as a PNG. Filler words removed automatically. A free, private, no-watermark alternative to wordart-style sites.
- /labs/resume-maker — Resume maker. Fill a form, pick one of five templates (ATS-safe single column, dark sidebar, accent banner, elegant serif, compact), add an optional photo and accent colour, and print to A4 — the print dialog is the download button. Live preview, localStorage autosave, every field optional. No sign-up, no watermark, no upload.
- /labs/biodata-maker — Marriage biodata maker. A matrimonial biodata rendered from a form into one of five templates (traditional maroon-and-gold through minimal black-on-white), with an optional photo and a selectable invocation line. Personal, horoscope, education, family, contact and partner-preference sections; empty fields simply do not render. Prints to A4, autosaves locally, nothing uploaded — deliberately, since a biodata carries birth details, income and a home address.
- /labs/processor-explorer — Inside a processor. Semantic-zoom journey from chip package to die to core pipeline to logic gate to a single transistor, with animated data flow at every level. Canvas 2D.
- /labs/hash-cracker — Live hash cracker. Watch a weak password hash fall in real time with a guesses-per-second counter, wordlist then brute force against MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256, in a Web Worker so the page stays responsive and Stop works instantly.
- /labs/algorithm-visualizer — Algorithm visualizer. Thirteen sorting algorithms and six pathfinding algorithms, animated and steppable, so O(n log n) beating O(n²) is shown rather than asserted.
- /labs/cpu-simulator — CPU & assembly simulator. Write assembly for a small clean instruction set and single-step it, watching registers, flags, memory and the stack change. A real two-pass assembler, no eval.
- /labs/shader-playground — GLSL shader playground. Write a fragment shader and see it render live on the GPU, with time and mouse uniforms and compile errors reported with line numbers.
- /labs/fractal-explorer — Fractal explorer. Zoom the Mandelbrot, Julia, Burning Ship and Tricorn sets smoothly on the GPU, with several colour palettes; hover to pick a Julia constant.

## Language playgrounds, terminals & HackLab

The rest of Labs. Real language runtimes compiled to WebAssembly and vendored
locally (no CDN), full operating systems under x86 emulation, and a deliberately
vulnerable XSS playground. Every playground below is a genuine compiler or
interpreter, not a sandbox that fakes output; the size given is the first-run
download, cached after that. They are listed by the year each language first
appeared, which is the order the picker and the hub use.

- /labs/c — C playground. Real clang compiled to WebAssembly and linked with lld, so structs, pointers, malloc and scanf behave as they do natively. The Input panel is wired to stdin. ~58 MB.
- /labs/sql — SQL playground. A real SQLite engine compiled to WebAssembly (sql.js). CREATE, INSERT and SELECT against an in-memory database, with results rendered as a table. ~700 KB.
- /labs/cpp — C++ playground. The same clang toolchain as the C lab, with libc++ — vector, string, map, algorithm and templates all compile, and stdin works. ~58 MB.
- /labs/perl — Perl playground. Real Perl 5 compiled to WebAssembly (WebPerl), including the regular expression engine that made the language famous. ~16 MB.
- /labs/python — Python playground. Genuine CPython compiled to WebAssembly (Pyodide), with the standard library and an input() that reads the Input panel. pip install is not available. ~12 MB.
- /labs/lua — Lua playground. Real Lua 5.4 compiled to WebAssembly (Wasmoon) — tables, metatables, coroutines and io.read. At ~420 KB it starts almost instantly.
- /labs/php — PHP playground. Real PHP 8.4 compiled to WebAssembly, with enums, match, readonly properties and the full array library. The opening <?php tag is added for you if you leave it out. ~14 MB.
- /labs/javascript — JavaScript playground. The browser's own JS engine, in a Web Worker, so there is nothing at all to download; whatever is typed in the Input panel arrives as stdin. 0 KB.
- /labs/ruby — Ruby playground. Real CRuby from the Ruby core team compiled to WebAssembly (ruby.wasm) — blocks, mixins and enumerables. ~17 MB.
- /labs/postgres — PostgreSQL playground. The actual PostgreSQL server compiled to WebAssembly (PGlite), not a Postgres-compatible reimplementation, so the dialect, the types and the error messages match a real install. Window functions, CTEs and JSONB. ~17 MB.
- /labs/typescript — TypeScript playground. The official tsc compiler doing real type checking, with type errors reported before anything executes; the emitted JavaScript then runs on the browser's own JS engine, reading the Input panel through stdin. ~9 MB.
- OS terminals: /labs/linux, /labs/dos (FreeDOS) and /labs/bsd (OpenBSD), each a real operating system booted under x86 emulation (v86) in the tab.
- /labs/leak — What your browser leaks. The public and local IP addresses any page can read out of WebRTC without a permission prompt, plus graphics card, time zone, CPU cores and a canvas fingerprint that survives clearing cookies, each with what it gives away and what can be done about it. Everything is computed in the tab with one exception the page states in print: reading the public IP means asking a public STUN server — Google's and Cloudflare's are both listed — which is a real request.
- /labs/api — HTTP API tester. Compose and send real HTTP requests and inspect the response, the one place in the offline set that intentionally reaches the network the visitor points it at.
- /labs/typing — Typing speed test. WPM and accuracy over configurable text, entirely offline.
- /labs/hacklab — HackLab. A safe, sandboxed target for practising web attacks (reflected and stored XSS against a deliberately vulnerable guestbook), with its own strict CSP isolating it from the rest of the site. For learning the offensive side in a place where breaking things is the point.

## Reading the site: search and themes

**Search.** Every page has a search button in the header. It runs against a prebuilt
index covering all 97 pages and opens a full-screen panel, on a phone and a laptop
alike. The index ships with the site and the matching happens in the tab, so no
search query is ever sent anywhere. Analytics is told only that a search ran and how
many results it returned — a zero-result count shows where the site is missing
something — never what was typed.

**Themes.** A light/dark toggle sits beside it. The site is dark by default and
light is opt-in — it deliberately does not follow the operating system setting,
because that would hand a light site to anyone with a light desktop without their
asking. The choice is stored locally and applied before the first paint, so a
returning visitor never sees the wrong theme flash.

Both themes are held to the WCAG AA contrast floor (4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for
large text) on every page. Elements that are dark instruments by design — the
terminals, the code editor, the visualiser canvases, HackLab's simulated corporate
portal — keep their dark palette in both themes rather than being re-coloured, so
they read the same either way.
